scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The genre traces its roots to the 1930s and 1940s, when Congolese musicians blended traditional rhythms with imported Cuban son and rumba.
By the 1960s, young musicians in Kinshasa and Brazzaville began speeding up these rhythms.

Orchestre Sinza Kotoko is credited with introducing the soukous style to Brazzaville nightlife around 1966, while bands like Zaïko Langa Langa later solidified the 'third school' of Congolese music with their fast-paced, free-form dance approach.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is a pillar of Congolese social life, central to weddings, popular festivals, and nightlife.
It serves as a medium for social commentary, love, and philosophical musing, with lyrics often performed in Lingala, Kikongo, French, or Swahili.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Soukous is characterized by rapid, rhythmic hip movements and shifting body weight between the legs.
Dancers often engage in freestyle sections during the sebene, where the music intensifies.
The dance is highly energetic, requiring fluid torso control and precise footwork that matches the fast-paced percussion and guitar lines.
Watch for Sebene dance.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music utilizes electric guitars, double bass, congas, and brass/woodwinds.
The lead guitar is central, known for speed and nimble fingerwork in the higher registers.

The pulse is 4/4 at about 128 beats a minute.
Bright, high-pitched electric guitar lines weaving through a fast, driving bassline and crisp percussion.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Soukous is primarily an urban dance performed in clubs, dance halls, and at large social gatherings like weddings and malakis.
Performers and dancers often emphasize elegance and fashion, a trend linked to the Sapeur movement, which prioritizes style even in difficult economic circumstances.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Franco Luambo and TPOK Jazz, Tabu Ley Rochereau, Docteur Nico, Papa Wemba, and Aurlus Mabélé.
Variants include the fast-paced ndombolo, the kiri-kiri dance style, and the Colombian champeta, which fuses soukous with local coastal culture.
Congolese rumba (parent) -> Soukous (child) -> Ndombolo/Champeta (variants).
